name: Chapter 13: Probability
description: Conditional probability, multiplication theorem, independent events, total probability and Bayes' theorem, with every exercise computed exactly and exam-style problems.

cards.term: Definition of conditional probability.
cards.definition: P(E|F) = P(E ∩ F)/P(F), P(F) ≠ 0: the probability of E given that F has occurred. F becomes the new (reduced) sample space

cards.term: Conditional probability: F becomes the new sample space
cards.definition: P(E|F) = P(E and F)/P(F); F becomes the reduced sample space; P(E|F) = 0.2/0.3 = 2/3 and P(F|E) = 1/3 for P(E)=0.6, P(F)=0.3, P(E and F)=0.2

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Conditional probability

P(E) = 0.6, P(F) = 0.3 and P(E ∩ F) = 0.2. Find P(E|F) and P(F|E). What does conditioning do to the sample space?

Restrict attention to F.
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Conditional probability

P(E) = 0.6, P(F) = 0.3 and P(E ∩ F) = 0.2. Find P(E|F) and P(F|E). What does conditioning do to the sample space?

P(E|F) = P(E ∩ F)/P(F) (P(F) ≠ 0): once F has occurred, F becomes the whole sample space, and we ask what fraction of it lies in E. Here 0.2/0.3 = 2/3; and P(F|E) = 0.2/0.6 = 1/3 (Ex 13.1 Q1).

Facts: 0 ≤ P(E|F) ≤ 1; P(E′|F) = 1 − P(E|F); P((E ∪ F)|G) = P(E|G) + P(F|G) − P((E ∩ F)|G). The conditional probability P(E|F) is generally different from P(F|E).

cards.term: Properties of conditional probability.
cards.definition: 0 ≤ P(E|F) ≤ 1; P(S|F) = P(F|F) = 1; P(E′|F) = 1 − P(E|F); P((E ∪ F)|G) = P(E|G) + P(F|G) − P((E ∩ F)|G); P(E|F) = 0 if E and F are mutually exclusive

cards.term: Trap: is P(E|F) the same as P(F|E)?
cards.definition: No: they share the numerator P(E ∩ F) but have different denominators. P(rain | clouds) ≠ P(clouds | rain). (Example 1 type: P(E|F) = 2/3, P(F|E) = 1/3)

cards.term: Two ways to compute a conditional probability.
cards.definition: 1) Formula P(E ∩ F)/P(F). 2) Reduce the sample space: count only outcomes in F and see how many are also in E (works when outcomes are equally likely)

cards.term: Conditional probability by counting the reduced sample space
cards.definition: Given black die 5, the sample space is the 6 outcomes with black=5; sum>9 happens for red=5,6 so probability 2/6 = 1/3; part (b): sum 8 given red<4 is 2/18 = 1/9

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Ex 13.1 Q10(a) · reduced sample space

A black and a red die are rolled. Find P(sum greater than 9 | the black die shows 5).

Only look at the row where the black die is 5.
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Ex 13.1 Q10(a) · reduced sample space

A black and a red die are rolled. Find P(sum greater than 9 | the black die shows 5).

Given “black = 5”, only the 6 outcomes in that row remain, equally likely. Sums greater than 9 occur for red = 5 and 6 (sums 10 and 11): 2 of 6 = 1/3.

Formula check: P(E ∩ F) = 2/36, P(F) = 6/36, so P(E|F) = 2/6. For (b), given red < 4, the sum 8 needs (6, 2) or (5, 3): 2 of 18 outcomes, 1/9.

cards.term: Example 2: a family has two children. P(both are boys | at least one is a boy)?
cards.definition: Sample space {BB, BG, GB, GG}. F = {BB, BG, GB}: 3 outcomes, E ∩ F = {BB}: 1/3. If instead the elder is known to be a boy the answer is 1/2 (F = {BB, BG})

cards.term: Example 6 type: a die is thrown twice; P(sum is 4 | numbers are different) etc.
cards.definition: Count in the reduced space. Different numbers: 30 outcomes; sum 4 with different numbers: (1,3), (3,1): 2/30 = 1/15 (Ex 13.1 Q14)
P(E|F) = 0.2/0.3 = 2/3; P(F|E) = 0.2/0.6 = 1/3

cards.term: Ex 13.1 Q2: compute P(A|B) if P(B) = 0.5 and P(A ∩ B) = 0.32.

cards.definition: (i) 0.8 × 0.4 = 0.32. (ii) 0.32/0.5 = 0.64. (iii) 0.8 + 0.5 − 0.32 = 0.98

cards.term: Ex 13.1 Q4: evaluate P(A ∪ B) if 2P(A) = P(B) = 5/13 and P(A|B) = 2/5.

Ex 13.1 Q6: a coin is tossed three times. Find P(E|F) for (i) E: head on third toss, F: heads on first two (ii) E: at least two heads, F: at most two heads (iii) E: at most two tails, F: at least one tail.
cards.definition: (i) F = {HHH, HHT}, E ∩ F = {HHH}: 1/2. (ii) F has 7 outcomes (all but HHH), E ∩ F = exactly two heads (3): 3/7. (iii) F has 7 outcomes (all but HHH), E ∩ F = one or two tails (6): 6/7

cards.term:
Ex 13.1 Q7: two coins are tossed once. Find P(E|F):
(i) E: tail on one coin, F: one coin shows head
(ii) E: no tail, F: no head.
cards.definition: (i) E = {HT, TH, TT}, F = {HT, TH, HH}: E ∩ F = {HT, TH}: 2/3. (ii) E = {HH}, F = {TT}: E ∩ F = ∅: 0

cards.term: Ex 13.1 Q8: a die is thrown three times. E: 4 on the third throw; F: 6 and 5 on the first two throws. Find P(E|F).
cards.definition: The third throw is independent of the first two: 1/6

cards.term: Ex 13.1 Q9: mother, father and son line up at random. E: son at one end; F: father in the middle. Find P(E|F).
cards.definition: With father in the middle the son is always at an end: 1

cards.term:
Ex 13.1 Q10(a),(b): black and red dice.
(a) P(sum > 9 | black die shows 5)
(b) P(sum = 8 | red die shows a number < 4).
cards.definition: (a) 1/3 (red = 5 or 6). (b) Red ∈ {1, 2, 3} gives 18 outcomes; sum 8 needs (black, red) = (6, 2) or (5, 3): 2/18 = 1/9

cards.term:
Ex 13.1 Q11: a die is rolled. E = {1, 3, 5}, F = {2, 3}, G = {2, 3, 4, 5}. Find
(i) P(E|F), P(F|E)
(ii) P(E|G), P(G|E)
(iii) P((E ∪ F)|G), P((E ∩ F)|G).
cards.definition: (i) 1/2, 1/3. (ii) E ∩ G = {3, 5}: 1/2 and 2/3. (iii) E ∪ F = {1, 2, 3, 5}, ∩ G = {2, 3, 5}: 3/4; E ∩ F = {3}: 1/4

cards.term:
Ex 13.1 Q12: each child is equally likely a boy or a girl. A family has two children. P(both girls) given
(i) the youngest is a girl
(ii) at least one is a girl.
cards.definition: (i) 1/2. (ii) {GG, GB, BG} → 1/3

cards.term: Ex 13.1 Q13: a bank has 300 true/false, 200 difficult true/false, 500 easy MCQs and 400 difficult MCQs. P(easy | it is an MCQ)?
cards.definition: MCQs total 900, easy MCQs 500: 5/9

cards.term: Ex 13.1 Q14: two dice are thrown and the numbers are different. Find P(sum is 4).
cards.definition: 30 outcomes with different numbers; sum 4: (1, 3), (3, 1): 1/15

cards.term: Ex 13.1 Q15: throw a die; if a multiple of 3 comes up, throw again; otherwise toss a coin. P(the coin shows a tail | at least one die shows 3).
cards.definition: The coin is only tossed when the first throw is not a multiple of 3 (no 3 has appeared then), so “at least one die shows 3” and “coin shows tail” cannot happen together: 0

cards.term:
Ex 13.1 Q16: if P(A) = ½ and P(B) = 0, then P(A|B) is
(A) 0
(B) ½ (C) not defined
(D) 1
cards.definition: Conditioning on an event of probability 0 is undefined: (C) not defined

cards.term:
Ex 13.1 Q17: if P(A|B) = P(B|A), then
(A) A ⊂ B but A ≠ B
(B) A = B
(C) A ∩ B = ∅
(D) P(A) = P(B)
cards.definition: P(A ∩ B)/P(B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(A) ⇒ P(A) = P(B) (when P(A ∩ B) ≠ 0): (D)

cards.term: Multiplication theorem of probability.
cards.definition: P(E ∩ F) = P(E) P(F|E) = P(F) P(E|F) (P(E), P(F) ≠ 0). For three events: P(E ∩ F ∩ G) = P(E) P(F|E) P(G|E ∩ F)

cards.term: Example 8: an urn has 10 black and 5 white balls. Two balls are drawn without replacement. P(both black)?
Example 9: three cards are drawn successively without replacement from a pack. P(first two kings and third an ace)?
Drawing with vs without replacement.
cards.definition: With replacement: draws are independent (same probabilities each time). Without replacement: the sample space shrinks, so use conditional probabilities (or combinations)

cards.term: Independent events: P(E ∩ F) = P(E)P(F)
cards.definition: E,F independent iff P(E and F) = P(E)P(F) iff P(E|F) = P(E); coin head and die 3 are independent (1/12 = 1/2 * 1/6); independent is different from mutually exclusive

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Independent events

A fair coin and a fair die are tossed. A: “head”, B: “3 on the die”. Are A and B independent?

Compare the overlap with the product of the two probabilities.
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Independent events

A fair coin and a fair die are tossed. A: “head”, B: “3 on the die”. Are A and B independent?

Events are independent if P(E ∩ F) = P(E) P(F), equivalently P(E|F) = P(E): learning that F happened does not change the chance of E. On the unit square, the overlap area equals the product of the two side lengths.

Here P(A ∩ B) = 1/12 = (1/2)(1/6): independent (Ex 13.2 Q4). Independence is not the same as mutually exclusive: exclusive events with positive probabilities are dependent (P(A ∩ B) = 0 ≠ P(A)P(B)).

cards.term: Definition of independent events.
cards.definition: E and F are independent if P(E ∩ F) = P(E) P(F). Equivalent (for P(F) ≠ 0): P(E|F) = P(E); (for P(E) ≠ 0): P(F|E) = P(F)

cards.term: Independent vs mutually exclusive.
cards.definition: Different ideas: mutually exclusive means E ∩ F = ∅ (so P(E ∩ F) = 0). Two exclusive events with positive probabilities can never be independent (0 ≠ P(E)P(F))

cards.term: If E and F are independent, which other pairs are independent?
cards.definition: E′ and F, E and F′, E′ and F′ (Example 13)

cards.term: Example 14: A, B independent. P(at least one occurs) = ?
cards.definition: 1 − P(A′)P(B′) = 1 − (1 − P(A))(1 − P(B))

cards.term: Independence of three events (pairwise vs mutual).
cards.definition:
A, B, C are mutually independent if P(A ∩ B ∩ C) = P(A)P(B)P(C) AND every pair is independent.
Pairwise independence alone is not enough

cards.term: Example 10: die thrown. E: multiple of 3; F: even. Independent?
cards.definition: P(E) = 2/6 = 1/3, P(F) = 1/2, P(E ∩ F) = P({6}) = 1/6 = (1/3)(1/2): independent

cards.term: Ex 13.2 Q1: A and B independent, P(A) = 3/5, P(B) = 1/5. Find P(A ∩ B).
cards.definition: 3/25 → 3/25

cards.term: Ex 13.2 Q2: two cards are drawn without replacement from a pack of 52. P(both black)?
Ex 13.2 Q3: three oranges are drawn without replacement from a box of 15 with 12 good and 3 bad. P(box approved) = P(all three good)?
Ex 13.2 Q4: a fair coin and an unbiased die are tossed. A: head; B: 3 on the die. Independent?
cards.definition: P(A ∩ B) = 1/12 = (1/2)(1/6): independent

cards.term: Ex 13.2 Q5: a die has faces 1, 2, 3 red and 4, 5, 6 green. A: even number; B: red. Independent?
cards.definition: P(A) = 1/2, P(B) = 1/2, P(A ∩ B) = P({2}) = 1/6 ≠ 1/4: not independent

cards.term: Ex 13.2 Q6: P(E) = 3/5, P(F) = 3/10, P(E ∩ F) = 1/5. Independent?
cards.definition: P(E)P(F) = 9/50 ≠ 1/5 = 10/50: not independent

cards.term:
Ex 13.2 Q7: P(A) = ½, P(A ∪ B) = 3/5, P(B) = p. Find p if
(i) A, B mutually exclusive
(ii) independent.
cards.definition: (i) 3/5 = 1/2 + p: p = 1/10. (ii) 3/5 = 1/2 + p − p/2 = 1/2 + p/2: p = 1/5

cards.term:
Ex 13.2 Q8: A and B independent, P(A) = 0.3, P(B) = 0.4. Find
(i) P(A ∩ B)
(ii) P(A ∪ B)
(iii) P(A|B)
(iv) P(B|A).
cards.definition: (i) 0.12 (ii) 0.3 + 0.4 − 0.12 = 0.58 (iii) P(A) = 0.3 (iv) P(B) = 0.4

cards.term: Ex 13.2 Q9: P(A) = ¼, P(B) = ½, P(A ∩ B) = 1/8. Find P(not A and not B).
Ex 13.2 Q10: P(A) = ½, P(B) = 7/12, P(not A or not B) = ¼. Independent?
cards.definition: P(A′ ∪ B′) = 1 − P(A ∩ B) would give P(A ∩ B) = 3/4, larger than P(A) = ½, so the data as printed are inconsistent. With the intended “neither” reading P(A′ ∩ B′) = 1/4: P(A ∪ B) = 3/4, P(A ∩ B) = ½ + 7/12 − 3/4 = 1/3 ≠ P(A)P(B) = 7/24. Either way the key’s answer is not independent

cards.term:
Ex 13.2 Q11: A, B independent with P(A) = 0.3, P(B) = 0.6. Find
(i) P(A and B)
(ii) P(A and not B)
(iii) P(A or B)
(iv) P(neither A nor B).
cards.definition: (i) 0.18 (ii) 0.3 × 0.4 = 0.12 (iii) 0.3 + 0.6 − 0.18 = 0.72 (iv) 0.7 × 0.4 = 0.28

cards.term: Ex 13.2 Q12: a die is tossed thrice. P(at least one odd number)?
cards.definition: 1 − (1/2)³ = 7/8

cards.term:
Ex 13.2 Q13: two balls drawn with replacement from 10 black and 8 red. Find P
(i) both red
(ii) first black, second red
(iii) one black, one red.
cards.definition: (i) (8/18)² = 16/81 (ii) (10/18)(8/18) = 20/81 (iii) 2 × 20/81 = 40/81

cards.term:
Ex 13.2 Q14: A and B solve a problem independently with probabilities ½ and ⅓. Find P
(i) solved
(ii) exactly one solves.

Ex 13.2 Q15: one card from a deck. In which cases are E and F independent?
(i) spade / ace
(ii) black / king
(iii) king or queen / queen or jack
cards.definition: (i) 13/52 · 4/52 = 1/52 = P(ace of spades) ✓ independent. (ii) 26/52 · 4/52 = 1/26 = 2/52 ✓ independent. (iii) 8/52 · 8/52 = 1/169 ≠ 4/52: (i) and (ii) are independent (iii) is not

cards.term:
Ex 13.2 Q16: in a hostel 60% read Hindi, 40% read English, 20% read both. Find
(a) P(neither)
(b) P(English | Hindi)
(c) P(Hindi | English).
cards.definition: (a) 1 − (0.6 + 0.4 − 0.2) = 1/5. (b) 0.2/0.6 = 1/3. (c) 0.2/0.4 = 1/2

cards.term:
Ex 13.2 Q17: P(even prime on each die when a pair of dice is rolled) is
(A) 0
(B) 1/3
(C) 1/12
(D) 1/36
cards.definition: The only even prime is 2: (1/6)(1/6) = (D) 1/36

cards.term:
Ex 13.2 Q18: two events A and B are independent if
(A) mutually exclusive
(B) P(A′B′) = [1 − P(A)][1 − P(B)]
(C) P(A) = P(B)
(D) P(A) + P(B) = 1
cards.definition: Independence of A and B is equivalent to that of A′ and B′: (B)

cards.term: Partition of a sample space: definition.
cards.definition: Events E₁, ..., Eₙ form a partition if Eᵢ ∩ Eⱼ = ∅ (i ≠ j), each P(Eᵢ) > 0, and E₁ ∪ ... ∪ Eₙ = S (they cover S with no overlap)

cards.term: Theorem of total probability.
cards.definition: P(A) = Σ P(Eᵢ) P(A|Eᵢ) for a partition {E₁, ..., Eₙ}: the probability of A is the weighted average over the “causes”

cards.term: Bayes’ theorem.
cards.definition: P(Eᵢ|A) = P(Eᵢ) P(A|Eᵢ) / Σⱼ P(Eⱼ) P(A|Eⱼ). It reverses the conditioning: from P(A|Eⱼ) (effect given cause) to P(Eᵢ|A) (cause given effect)

cards.term: How to set up a Bayes problem (4 steps).
cards.definition: 1) Name the causes E₁, ..., Eₙ and the observed event A. 2) Write the priors P(Eᵢ). 3) Write the likelihoods P(A|Eᵢ). 4) Compute the total P(A) and then P(Eᵢ|A) = prior × likelihood ÷ total

cards.term: Tree diagram: total probability and Bayes
cards.definition: Total probability P(A) = sum P(Ei)P(A|Ei); Bayes P(Ei|A) = P(Ei)P(A|Ei)/P(A); machines A (60%,2%) and B (40%,1%): P(B|defective) = 1/4

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Probability tree

Machine A makes 60% of the items (2% defective) and machine B makes 40% (1% defective). An item chosen at random is defective. What is the probability that it came from B?

Multiply along the branches, add the two defective paths.
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Probability tree

Machine A makes 60% of the items (2% defective) and machine B makes 40% (1% defective). An item chosen at random is defective. What is the probability that it came from B?

Total probability: P(defective) = 0.6 × 0.02 + 0.4 × 0.01 = 0.012 + 0.004 = 0.016 (multiply along a branch, add the branches that lead to “defective”).

Bayes: P(B | defective) = 0.004/0.016 = 1/4 (Ex 13.3 Q8). Reading a tree: the probability of a full path is the product of its branch probabilities; conditional probabilities are “branch ÷ total”.

cards.term: Bayes: why rare-disease tests give many false positives
cards.definition: Bayes theorem P(Ei|A) = P(Ei)P(A|Ei)/sum P(Ej)P(A|Ej); with prevalence 0.1%, sensitivity 99% and false positive 0.5%, P(disease | +) = 22/133 = 16.5%

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Bayes' theorem in natural frequencies

A test detects the disease 99% of the time, but gives a false positive for 0.5% of healthy people. If 0.1% of people have the disease, what is P(disease | test positive)?

Imagine a population of 100 000 people.
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Bayes' theorem in natural frequencies

A test detects the disease 99% of the time, but gives a false positive for 0.5% of healthy people. If 0.1% of people have the disease, what is P(disease | test positive)?

Think of 100 000 people: 100 have the disease and 99 of them test positive; of the 99 900 healthy people about 0.5% ≈ 500 also test positive. Among ≈ 599 positives only 99 are ill: 99/599 ≈ 16.5%. Exactly: 0.001·0.99/(0.001·0.99 + 0.999·0.005) = 22/133 (Ex 13.3 Q5).

Bayes’ theorem: P(Eᵢ|A) = P(Eᵢ)P(A|Eᵢ)/Σⱼ P(Eⱼ)P(A|Eⱼ). A rare disease means most positives are false alarms, even for a good test.

cards.term: Trap: confusing P(A|B) with P(B|A) (the prosecutor’s fallacy).
cards.definition: A test being 99% accurate does not mean a positive result is 99% likely to be right: P(disease | +) ≠ P(+ | disease). The base rate (prior) matters

cards.term: Ex 13.3 Q1: an urn has 5 red and 5 black balls. A ball is drawn, its colour noted and returned with 2 more balls of the same colour, then a second ball is drawn. P(second is red)?
Ex 13.3 Q2: bag I has 4 red, 4 black; bag II has 2 red, 6 black. A bag is chosen at random and a red ball is drawn. P(it came from bag I)?
Ex 13.3 Q3: 60% of students are hostlers, 40% day scholars. 30% of hostlers and 20% of day scholars get grade A. A random student has grade A. P(hostler)?
Ex 13.3 Q4: P(student knows the answer) = 3/4, guesses with probability 1/4; a guess is correct with probability 1/4. P(knows | correct)?
Ex 13.3 Q5: a test detects the disease with probability 0.99 but has a 0.5% false positive rate; 0.1% of people have the disease. P(disease | positive)?
cards.definition: 22/133 ≈ 0.165 (see the frequency picture)

cards.term: Ex 13.3 Q6: three coins: two-headed, 75%-heads biased, and fair. One is chosen at random and shows heads. P(it is the two-headed coin)?
Ex 13.3 Q7: 2000 scooter, 4000 car and 6000 truck drivers are insured; accident probabilities 0.01, 0.03, 0.15. An insured person has an accident. P(scooter driver)?
Ex 13.3 Q8: machine A makes 60% of the items (2% defective), B makes 40% (1% defective). A defective item is chosen. P(it came from B)?

Ex 13.3 Q9: two groups win a board election with probabilities 0.6 and 0.4. If the first wins, a new product is introduced with probability 0.7; if the second wins, 0.3. Given a new product was introduced, P(the second group introduced it)?
Ex 13.3 Q10: a girl throws a die. If she gets 5 or 6 she tosses a coin three times; if 1, 2, 3 or 4 she tosses it once. She gets exactly one head. P(she threw 1, 2, 3 or 4)?
cards.definition: P(1 head | coin once) = 1/2 and P(1 head | three tosses) = 3/8: (2/3 · 1/2)/(2/3 · 1/2 + 1/3 · 3/8) = 8/11

cards.term: Ex 13.3 Q11: operators A (50% of the time), B (30%), C (20%) produce 1%, 5%, 7% defective items. A defective item is produced. P(it was produced by A)?
Ex 13.3 Q12: a card from a pack of 52 is lost. Two cards drawn from the remaining are both diamonds. P(the lost card was a diamond)?
cards.definition: Lost diamond (1/4): remaining 12 diamonds: C(12, 2). Lost non-diamond (3/4): 13 diamonds: C(13, 2). 11/50

cards.term:
Ex 13.3 Q13: A speaks the truth with probability 4/5. A coin is tossed and A reports a head. P(a head actually appeared) is
(A) 4/5
(B) 1/2
(C) 1/5
(D) 2/5

Ex 13.3 Q14: if A ⊂ B and P(B) ≠ 0, which is correct?
(A) P(A|B) = P(B)/P(A)
(B) P(A|B) < P(A)
(C) P(A|B) ≥ P(A)
(D) none
cards.definition: A ∩ B = A, so P(A|B) = P(A)/P(B) ≥ P(A) since P(B) ≤ 1: (C)

cards.term: Example 22: four boxes hold coloured balls (black counts 3 of 18, 2 of 8, 1 of 7, 4 of 13). A black ball is drawn from a random box. P(it came from box III)?
cards.definition: Bayes: (1/7)/(3/18 + 2/8 + 1/7 + 4/13) = 156/947 (the four boxes each have prior 1/4, which cancels)

cards.term: Example 24: a machine set up correctly gives 90% acceptable items, incorrectly set gives 40%. It is correctly set up 80% of the time. After a set-up it produces 2 acceptable items. P(correct set-up)?

Misc Q1: A and B with P(A) ≠ 0. Find P(B|A) if
(i) A ⊂ B
(ii) A ∩ B = ∅.
cards.definition: (i) P(A ∩ B) = P(A): 1. (ii) P(A ∩ B) = 0: 0

cards.term:
Misc Q2: a couple has two children.
(i) P(both males | at least one male)
(ii) P(both females | the elder is female).
cards.definition: (i) 1/3 (ii) 1/2

cards.term: Misc Q3: 5% of men and 0.25% of women have grey hair. A grey-haired person is chosen (equal numbers of men and women). P(male)?
Misc Q4: 90% of people are right-handed. P(at most 6 of a random sample of 10 are right-handed)?
cards.definition: By the binomial law: 1 − Σ (r = 7 to 10) ¹⁰Cᵣ (0.9)ʳ (0.1)¹⁰⁻ʳ ≈ 0.0128

cards.term: Misc Q5: a leap year is selected at random. P(it has 53 Tuesdays)?
cards.definition: A leap year has 52 weeks plus 2 extra days; the pair (extra days) is one of 7 equally likely pairs and Tuesday appears in 2 of them: 2/7

cards.term: Misc Q6: boxes A (1 red, 6 white, 3 black), B (6, 2, 2), C (8, 1, 1), D (0, 6, 4). A box is chosen at random and a red marble is drawn. P(box A), P(box B), P(box C)?
cards.definition: Red counts 1, 6, 8, 0 out of 10 each; total 15 red-weights: 1/15, 2/5, 8/15 (box D has no red marble)

cards.term: Misc Q7: heart-attack chance 40%; meditation and yoga reduce it by 30%, a drug by 25%. A patient chooses either at random and has an attack. P(he followed meditation and yoga)?
cards.definition: Attack probabilities 0.4 × 0.7 = 0.28 (meditation) and 0.4 × 0.75 = 0.30 (drug): 0.28/(0.28 + 0.30) = 14/29

cards.term: Misc Q8: each entry of a 2 × 2 determinant is 0 or 1 with probability ½ each. P(the determinant is positive)?
cards.definition: ad − bc > 0 needs ad = 1, bc = 0: (1/4)(3/4) = 3/16

cards.term:

cards.term: Misc Q12: if P(A|B) > P(A), then (A) P(B|A) < P(B) (B) P(A ∩ B) < P(A)P(B) (C) P(B|A) > P(B) (D) P(B|A) = P(B)
cards.definition: P(A ∩ B) > P(A)P(B), so P(B|A) = P(A ∩ B)/P(A) > P(B): (C)

cards.definition: P(A ∪ B) = P(A) forces P(B) = P(A ∩ B): (B) P(A|B) = 1

cards.term: Addition rule and its conditional form.
cards.definition: P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B); for independent events P(A ∪ B) = 1 − P(A′)P(B′)

cards.term: “At least one” problems.
cards.definition: Use the complement: P(at least one) = 1 − P(none). For n independent trials with success p: 1 − (1 − p)ⁿ

cards.term: Probability of exactly r successes in n independent trials (preview of the binomial law).
cards.definition: ⁿCᵣ pʳ (1 − p)ⁿ⁻ʳ. Example: exactly 2 heads in 3 tosses = 3 × (1/2)³ = 3/8

cards.term: Odds and probability.
cards.definition: If the odds in favour of A are a : b then P(A) = a/(a + b). Odds against: b : a

cards.term: A and B throw a die alternately; the first to get a 6 wins. A starts. P(A wins)?
Given P(A) = 0.5, P(B) = 0.3, P(A ∪ B) = 0.65. Are A and B independent?
cards.definition: P(A ∩ B) = 0.5 + 0.3 − 0.65 = 0.15 = 0.5 × 0.3: independent

cards.term: A bag has 3 red and 2 blue balls. Two balls are drawn without replacement. P(second is blue | first is red)?
cards.definition: After a red is removed: 2 red, 2 blue: 2/4 = 1/2

cards.term: Bayes with two urns: which urn is more likely if a white ball is drawn?
cards.definition:
Compare the numerators P(urn) × P(white | urn); with equal priors the urn with the larger proportion of white balls is more likely.
Divide by the total to get exact probabilities

cards.term:
Assertion–Reason.
A: P(A|B) + P(A′|B) = 1.
R: conditional probabilities behave like ordinary probabilities on the reduced sample space.
(a) Both true, R explains A (b) Both true, R does not (c) A true, R false (d) A false, R true
cards.definition: (a)

cards.term:
Assertion–Reason.
A: if A and B are mutually exclusive events with positive probabilities, they are independent.
R: P(A ∩ B) = 0 for mutually exclusive events.
(a) Both true, R explains A (b) A false, R true (c) A true, R false (d) Both false
cards.definition: (b): P(A)P(B) > 0 = P(A ∩ B)

cards.term: True/False: P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B|A) always (P(A) ≠ 0).

cards.term: True/False: if P(A|B) = P(A) then P(B|A) = P(B) (P(A), P(B) > 0).
cards.definition: True: both mean P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B)
